conventions.sources: ids refer to the numbered source lists (S1…S108) in the markdown dossier
conventions.whenAlso: optional when.also = second predicate on another marker (markerId), a profile/plan field (field), or {repeat:true} = confirmed on a repeat test
conventions.symbolicValues: whoCutoff (13.0 g/dL men, 12.0 g/dL women), labLow/labHigh/labRange = the range printed on the report
conventions.grades: A meta-analysis or several concordant RCTs; B few RCTs or consistent human data; C limited or indirect human; D mechanism, animal or expert opinion (R5 policy: grades set band width and wording, never gate)

ranges.note: Indian reference cut-offs 1–2 g/dL lower than WHO, children 1–19 y only; adults use WHO

clinicianOnly.message: Haemoglobin below 8 g/dL is severe anaemia. Please see a clinician before any deficit or fast.
Haemoglobin above your lab's range needs a clinician to look at it (dehydration, smoking, altitude or a blood disorder).

ranges.note: iron deficiency when inflammation is present
low stores in athletes; practice, not consensus
overload risk, men and non-menstruating women (not on ferritin alone)

clinicianOnly.message: Ferritin below 15 means your iron stores are empty. Please ask a clinician about iron treatment and the cause.
Ferritin above 200 (men) or 150 (women) with a normal CRP needs a clinician to check for iron overload. Vitals stops suggesting iron.

ranges.note: pg/mL (= 100 pmol/L) proposed for young Indian vegetarians; single study

clinicianOnly.message: B12 this low (below about 100 pmol/L) should be treated by a clinician, sooner if you have numbness, tingling or memory problems.

ranges.note: ng/mL; toxicity only with hypercalcaemia; hallmark >150

clinicianOnly.message: Vitamin D above 100 ng/mL is in the toxic range for some people. Stop vitamin D supplements and ask a clinician to check your calcium.

ranges.note: mg/L; above 10 = probable acute inflammation, repeat

clinicianOnly.message: hs-CRP above 10 on two tests a few weeks apart needs a clinician to look for the cause.

ranges.note: use the lab's printed range; AACE/ATA treat-threshold discussion at 10 mIU/L
µIU/mL; hypothyroid cut-off used in the 8-city study

clinicianOnly.message: TSH above 10 usually means an under-active thyroid that is treated. Please see a clinician.
TSH below your lab's range can mean an over-active thyroid or too much thyroid medicine. Please see a clinician.

ranges.note: use the lab range; free T3 ~2.0–4.4 pg/mL typical, assay dependent

clinicianOnly.message: Free T3 above your lab's range can mean an over-active thyroid. Please see a clinician.
Testosterone below 264 ng/dL on two morning tests needs a clinician, especially with low libido, low energy or loss of morning erections.

ranges.note: µg/dL morning; below suggests adrenal insufficiency (with ACTH)
morning serum cortisol is not a Cushing's screening test

clinicianOnly.message: A morning cortisol below 5 µg/dL can mean the adrenal glands are not making enough. Please see a clinician soon, before any fasting.
A high morning cortisol on its own is not a diagnosis. If your doctor ordered it, discuss it with them.

interactions.effectSize: no trial of Hb found
interactions.mechanism: Low carbohydrate raises resting and post-exercise hepcidin (S17, S18), which lowers iron absorption; any Hb effect would take months and only in low-iron people (expectation)

interactions.effectSize: no Hb trial; vegetarians have ferritin −29.7 µg/L vs omnivores
interactions.mechanism: Meat/fish protein brings haem iron; plant protein brings phytate-bound iron (expectation for Hb)

interactions.effectSize: no data in healthy adults; Hb < 8 g/dL is a reason not to fast (Ramadan review)
interactions.mechanism: Fasting reduces iron, B12 and folate intake; harm in severe anaemia is expert opinion

interactions.effectSize: coffee −39 %, tea −64 % non-haem iron absorption from the same meal; no effect 1 h before
interactions.mechanism: Polyphenols (chlorogenic acid, tannins) chelate non-haem iron in the gut; Hb falls only if stores run down (months)

interactions.effectSize: no effect of 25 % CR over 24 months on Hb or hepcidin
interactions.population: non-obese adults with an 18 mg iron multivitamin
interactions.mechanism: Red-cell production is protected when micronutrients are covered; untested without the multivitamin and in already-anaemic people

interactions.effectSize: as above
interactions.mechanism: As above

interactions.effectSize: ΔHb vs Δplasma volume r = −0.81; transient haemolysis after long runs
interactions.mechanism: Training expands plasma volume (dilution) and foot-strike haemolysis destroys a few red cells; normalises 3–5 days after stopping

interactions.effectSize: no effect over 24 months of CR
interactions.mechanism: As deficit_large

interactions.effectSize: +0.42 g/dL (95 % CI 0.10–0.74); ≥ 1 g/dL in 2 weeks if iron-deficient
interactions.mechanism: Supplies iron for erythropoiesis; alternate-day dosing raises fractional absorption (21.8 vs 16.3 %)

interactions.effectSize: larger Hb rise at 4 and 8 weeks when B12 added to iron + folic acid
interactions.mechanism: B12 is needed for DNA synthesis in red-cell precursors; helps only if B12 is low

interactions.effectSize: 300–600 mg calcium with a meal cuts iron absorption 50–60 %
interactions.mechanism: Calcium inhibits both haem and non-haem iron uptake at the enterocyte; separate from iron-rich meals

interactions.effectSize: no ferritin trial; hepcidin higher after 24 h at 3 g/kg CHO and after 6 days LCHF
interactions.mechanism: Low muscle glycogen raises exercise IL-6, which drives hepatic hepcidin and blocks iron absorption for hours after training

interactions.effectSize: vegetarians −29.7 µg/L vs omnivores
interactions.mechanism: Animal protein brings better-absorbed haem iron (classic physiology); plant protein does not; direction depends on the source

interactions.effectSize: ferritin and serum iron rise progressively with intake; beer more than wine or spirits
interactions.mechanism: Alcohol suppresses hepcidin and injures liver cells; a high ferritin then overstates stores

interactions.effectSize: coffee −39 %, tea −64 % (up to −94 % for black tea) of meal iron absorbed
interactions.mechanism: Polyphenol chelation of non-haem iron in the gut; separating by ≥ 1 h removes the effect

interactions.effectSize: 25 % CR for 24 months: no ferritin or hepcidin change; LEA alone did not raise hepcidin over 6 days
interactions.population: non-obese adults with multivitamin; elite race walkers
interactions.mechanism: Stores are protected when iron intake is covered; less food means less iron if the diet is not iron-dense

interactions.effectSize: as above
interactions.mechanism: As above

interactions.effectSize: hepcidin 1.7–3.1× at 3–24 h after a 60-min run; iron deficiency in 15–35 % of female and 5–11 % of male athletes
interactions.mechanism: Exercise IL-6 → hepcidin → less iron absorbed, plus sweat, gut and haemolysis losses

interactions.effectSize: no change over 24 months of CR
interactions.mechanism: Loss of inflammatory fat could lower ferritin in obesity (expectation)

interactions.effectSize: +12.6 ng/mL (95 % CI 8.3–16.9); alternate-day 60 mg absorbs 21.8 % vs 16.3 % daily
interactions.mechanism: Direct repletion; daily dosing raises hepcidin and blunts the next day's absorption

interactions.effectSize: 300–600 mg calcium with a meal cuts iron absorption 50–60 %
interactions.mechanism: Calcium inhibits enterocyte iron uptake; take calcium away from iron-rich meals

interactions.effectSize: CALERIE used an 18 mg iron multivitamin; no ferritin change in either arm
interactions.mechanism: Covers iron needs during restriction

interactions.effectSize: plasma B12 plateaus at ~10 µg/day intake; dairy and fish the main contributors
interactions.mechanism: Animal protein foods carry B12; plant protein carries none

interactions.effectSize: no egg-specific estimate found
interactions.mechanism: Eggs carry B12 (less bioavailable than dairy, expectation); lacto-ovo vegetarians fare better than vegans

interactions.effectSize: no whey-specific estimate; dairy B12 appears more bioavailable
interactions.mechanism: Whey is a dairy fraction carrying some B12 (expectation for magnitude)

interactions.effectSize: 647–1032 µg/day oral gives 80–90 % of the maximal MMA fall
interactions.mechanism: Passive (non-intrinsic-factor) absorption of ~1 % of a large oral dose

interactions.effectSize: 25(OH)D rose at 3 months on a ketogenic diet
interactions.mechanism: Unclear; possibly supplement use in the trial and fat loss (expectation)

interactions.effectSize: via weight loss: +3.3 ng/mL at 10–15 % and +7.7 at ≥ 15 % loss
interactions.mechanism: Volumetric dilution reverses as body size falls

interactions.effectSize: via weight loss: +2.1 to +2.7 ng/mL at < 10 % loss
interactions.mechanism: As above

interactions.effectSize: obese vs normal-weight 25(OH)D −19.8 nmol/L (≈ −8 ng/mL) at the same dose
interactions.mechanism: Larger body volume dilutes vitamin D

interactions.effectSize: exercise-only arm no different from control
interactions.mechanism: Outdoor training adds sun exposure (expectation, not measured)
Volumetric dilution

interactions.effectSize: ≈ +7 ng/mL per 1000 IU/day at baseline ~28 ng/mL; +4.8 per 1000 IU at low doses, flattening; obese need 2–3× the dose
interactions.mechanism: Substrate supply to hepatic 25-hydroxylase; half-life 15 days, plateau in ~2–3 months

interactions.effectSize: raised 25(OH)D near 30 ng/mL baseline, lowered it at 30–50
interactions.mechanism: Magnesium is a cofactor for vitamin D hydroxylases and catabolism

interactions.effectSize: no significant CRP effect (44 RCTs); IL-6 and TNF-α fell
interactions.mechanism: Ketosis may blunt inflammasome activity; CRP benefit tracks weight loss rather than carbohydrate

interactions.effectSize: IF −0.29 mg/L in one meta-analysis; no effect in another
interactions.mechanism: Benefit mostly through weight loss

interactions.effectSize: −0.14 mg/L per 1 %E less SFA (cross-sectional); top SFA quartile OR 1.58 for raised CRP
interactions.population: urban Asian Indian youth; US adults
interactions.mechanism: SFA activates TLR4 signalling in fat and immune cells (mechanism moderate)

interactions.effectSize: −0.37 mg/L (−0.74 to 0) when fibre rises ≥ 8 g/day
interactions.mechanism: Fermentation to short-chain fatty acids, lower gut-derived endotoxin, weight loss

interactions.effectSize: marine n-3 lowers CRP (68 RCTs); magnitude in mg/L not extracted
interactions.mechanism: n-3 fatty acids are precursors of pro-resolving mediators and reduce NF-κB signalling

interactions.effectSize: −0.13 mg/L per kg lost across all interventions
interactions.mechanism: Less visceral fat → less IL-6 → less hepatic CRP

interactions.effectSize: CR SMD −0.15; lifestyle slope ≈ −0.06 mg/L per kg
interactions.mechanism: As above

interactions.effectSize: no direct CRP data; overfeeding raised endotoxin markers
interactions.mechanism: Fat gain raises adipose IL-6 (expectation from the weight-loss slope)

interactions.effectSize: training of all types: ES 0.26
interactions.mechanism: Chronic training lowers IL-6 and visceral fat

interactions.effectSize: chronic: ES 0.26 lower (0.38 with weight loss); acute marathon: raised from day 1 to day 3
interactions.mechanism: Training is anti-inflammatory over weeks; muscle damage after long or hard sessions drives an acute-phase rise

interactions.effectSize: raised after 88 h awake and after 10 days at 4.2 h/night (mg/L not in abstract)
interactions.mechanism: Sleep loss activates sympathetic and IL-6 pathways

interactions.effectSize: −0.13 mg/L per kg (all); ≈ −0.06 per kg with lifestyle only

interactions.effectSize: CRP lowered (68 RCTs); umbrella ES −0.40, very heterogeneous

interactions.effectSize: −1.08 mg/L, larger if baseline ≥ 5 mg/L; another meta-analysis null

interactions.effectSize: covered by the fibre estimate

interactions.effectSize: as above

interactions.mechanism: As above

interactions.effectSize: obese TSH 3.3 vs 2.1 µU/mL in lean controls (association)

interactions.effectSize: 28 % loss: 2.33 → 1.82 µIU/mL; obese 3.3 → 2.1 after surgery

interactions.effectSize: 8 weeks: TSH fell and T3/T4 rose vs placebo

interactions.effectSize: separate from levothyroxine (4 h is traditional, untested)

interactions.effectSize: as calcium

interactions.effectSize: total T3 −24 to −55 % by 60 h; pooled fasting FT3 g = −1.98

rules.message: Because your haemoglobin was {value} g/dL on {date}, below the usual cut-off, your deficit is capped 5 points lower than usual until a retest.
Because your haemoglobin was {value} g/dL on {date}, fasts are kept to 24 hours or less until it is back in range.
Your haemoglobin was {value} g/dL on {date}. Low iron and low B12 are the common causes; add ferritin and B12 from the same report if you have them.
Endurance training dilutes the blood, so haemoglobin reads a little lower; your value of {value} g/dL on {date} is still below the cut-off, so a clinician check is worthwhile.
Because your haemoglobin was {value} g/dL on {date}, please see a clinician before starting a deficit or fasting. The plan stays at maintenance until then.
Retest haemoglobin in 4 weeks if you start iron, otherwise in 12 weeks.
Because your haemoglobin was {value} g/dL on {date}: drink tea or coffee at least an hour away from main meals; it blocks iron from food.
Because your ferritin was {value} ng/mL on {date}, your deficit is kept moderate (no more than 20 %) while you train for endurance.
Because your ferritin was {value} ng/mL on {date}: keep tea and coffee at least an hour away from meals; with meals they cut iron absorption by 40–60 %.
Because your ferritin was {value} ng/mL on {date}, recipes pair pulses and greens with a vitamin C food (lemon, amla, tomato) to absorb more iron.
Because your ferritin was {value} ng/mL on {date}, iron is shown in your supplement options; take it only with a clinician's advice, ideally on alternate days.
Calcium blocks iron absorption; take calcium at a different meal from iron-rich food or iron tablets.
Your CRP was raised when ferritin was measured on {date}; ferritin rises with inflammation, so {value} ng/mL may hide low iron. Retest when well.
Because your ferritin was {value} ng/mL on {date}, your iron stores are empty. Please see a clinician about treatment and the cause.
Because your ferritin was {value} ng/mL on {date} with a normal CRP, Vitals will not suggest iron; please ask a clinician about it.
Retest ferritin (with CRP) in 12 weeks, at least 2 weeks after any illness or hard race.
Because your B12 was {value} pg/mL on {date}, vitamin B12 is suggested in your supplements. Dairy, eggs and fish also help.
Your B12 was {value} pg/mL on {date}, borderline. Do you take metformin or an acid-reducing medicine (PPI)? Both lower B12; a clinician can confirm with an MMA or homocysteine test.
Because your B12 was {value} pg/mL on {date}, very low, please see a clinician, sooner if you have numbness, tingling or memory problems.
Because your B12 was {value} pg/mL on {date}, meals favour curd, milk, paneer and eggs where your diet allows.
Retest B12 about 12 weeks after starting a supplement.
Because your vitamin D was {value} ng/mL on {date}, low by Indian and international cut-offs, vitamin D3 is suggested in your supplements.
Your vitamin D was {value} ng/mL on {date}. A daily 600–1000 IU supplement or regular midday sun is optional; most adults at this level do not need more.
Because your vitamin D was {value} ng/mL on {date}, Vitals stops suggesting vitamin D. Please ask a clinician to check your calcium.
At a higher body weight the same vitamin D dose raises blood levels less; your value was {value} ng/mL on {date}.
Optional: recheck vitamin D about 12 weeks after starting a supplement. Routine yearly testing is not needed.
Because your hs-CRP was {value} mg/L on {date}, which usually means a recent illness, fasts are kept to 24 hours or less for 4 weeks.
Repeat hs-CRP in about 2 weeks when you feel well; a value above 10 is usually from an infection.
Because your hs-CRP was {value} mg/L on {date}, the plan ranks weight loss, fibre and regular training higher; they lower it.
Was the blood taken within 3 days of a hard race or session, or during a cold? Either can raise CRP for a few days.
Because your hs-CRP was {value} mg/L on {date}, cooking fats lean toward mustard, groundnut or olive oil rather than ghee or coconut oil.
Your hs-CRP has been above 10 mg/L on two tests ({date}). Please see a clinician to find the cause.
Because your TSH was {value} µIU/mL on {date}, outside your lab's range, please see a clinician. Your plan continues; it is not changed by this value.
Because your TSH was {value} µIU/mL on {date} and you are not on treatment, fasts are kept to 24 hours or less until a clinician has seen it.
Take levothyroxine with water 60 minutes before breakfast and coffee or tea; keep calcium and iron at least 4 hours away.
Ashwagandha can raise thyroid hormones. If you have a thyroid condition or take levothyroxine, check with your clinician first.
High-dose biotin (hair and nail products) can make thyroid results wrong. Stop it at least 24 hours before your next blood test.
Repeat TSH in about 8 weeks, or as your clinician advises.
Because your free T3 was {value} pg/mL on {date}, low, while your energy intake is very low for your training, Vitals suggests a 1–2 week diet break at maintenance.
Your free T3 was {value} pg/mL on {date}. T3 falls during fasting and very-low-carb eating to save energy; this is expected and reverses when you eat normally.
Because your free T3 ({value} pg/mL) and testosterone were both low on {date}, your deficit is capped at moderate and a diet break is scheduled.
Is this free T3 or total T3? Reports from camp panels usually show total T3 (in ng/dL).
Recheck free T3 about 4 weeks after a diet break or return to maintenance, not during a fast.
Your testosterone was {value} ng/dL on {date}. One value is not enough: repeat a fasting test before 10 am within 4 weeks, at the same lab.
Your testosterone has been below 264 ng/dL on two morning tests ({date}). Please see a clinician.
Because your testosterone was {value} ng/dL on {date} during a large deficit, the deficit is capped at moderate and a diet break is suggested; this usually recovers with more food.
Because your testosterone was {value} ng/dL on {date} and you sleep under 6 hours, sleep is the first lever: one week of 5-hour nights lowers it 10–15 %.
Because your testosterone was {value} ng/dL on {date}, protein stays at or below 3.4 g/kg and very-low-carb plans keep enough fat.
Because your testosterone was {value} ng/dL on {date}, losing weight is the lever most likely to raise it (about +3 nmol/L with diet).
Because your morning cortisol was {value} µg/dL on {date}, very low, please see a clinician soon. Fasting is paused until then.
Because your morning cortisol was {value} µg/dL on {date}, fasts are capped at 12 hours until a clinician has reviewed it.
A single morning cortisol changes with sleep, caffeine, fasting and exercise, so Vitals shows it but does not plan on it.
Was the sample taken after poor sleep, a fast, coffee, hard exercise, or while on steroid medicines or the pill? All raise cortisol.
